Bank Text Messages Not Arriving? How to Fix It and Spot Scams

Why your UK bank verification codes or 2FA texts aren't arriving — and what to do about it.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-05-07 · 5 min read

Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Report it — call Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland: 101), and forward scam texts to 7726.

Why your bank verification text might not be arriving

If your bank verification code or 2FA text has stopped arriving, possible causes include weak signal, phone settings, a blocked message, or a delay at the bank or mobile network. A SIM-swap or number-porting fraud is another possibility, but missing bank texts on their own do not prove that has happened. This guide starts with low-risk checks, then explains when to contact the bank and mobile network.

Quick fixes that work for any UK bank or service

Try restarting the phone, checking signal and Airplane Mode, looking in blocked or filtered messages, and requesting a new code once. Settings and menu names vary by phone. If other texts and calls work but the bank code does not, contact the bank through its app or the number on your card; ask whether it can offer an alternative verification method.

UK bank reference: sender IDs and how to verify a real bank message

Banks may use named sender IDs, but a sender name can be spoofed or hijacked and may appear in the same message thread as genuine texts. A mismatch is a warning sign, but a match is not proof. Treat any unexpected link asking you to log in, “verify” or enter security information as suspicious. Open the bank’s app yourself or type its address directly into the browser, and use the number on your card if you need to check a message.

Do not use a sender-ID list as proof

There is no safe universal list of bank sender IDs: banks can use more than one sender and may change their messaging arrangements. Do not treat a named sender, a message thread or a partial personal detail as authentication. Verify in the official app or through a trusted contact route instead.

Skip SMS: use app-based codes for banks and 2FA services

Some banks and online services offer in-app approval, an authenticator app, or another recovery method, but the options differ. Check the provider's official help page or app rather than assuming a particular method is available. Never install an authenticator app or approve a login because an unexpected caller tells you to.

When the bank or service network is at fault

Sometimes the problem isn't your phone or settings — it's the sending side. Bank SMS gateways occasionally have operational delays where text delivery to certain UK networks slows or stops temporarily. Mobile operators sometimes flag legitimate sender IDs as spam after a flood of malicious texts, blocking real bank messages alongside scams. UK government services like HMRC and NHS Digital have had similar SMS delivery issues during peak load (self-assessment deadline windows, vaccine appointment booking surges).

If your phone is otherwise working normally — texts from friends arrive, calls work, mobile data works — but only specific service messages aren't appearing, the issue is on their end. The fix isn't on your phone. Call the service on a verified number (from the back of your card or their official website) to ask whether there's a known SMS issue, and arrange an alternative method of verification while it's resolved.

When missing codes could indicate something more serious

Missing bank or 2FA texts on their own can have routine causes. If you also see unexplained “no service” or “SOS only”, calls fail, mobile data stops or texts from other people do not arrive, contact your mobile network and bank promptly because a SIM swap or number port is one possible explanation. Missing codes alone do not establish that a SIM swap has happened.

What to do if you see those warning signs

If the phone suddenly shows no service or SOS only, calls fail, or messages from other people also stop, use another phone to contact the bank and mobile network on verified numbers. Ask whether a SIM replacement or number port has been requested and secure the affected accounts. Report suspected fraud to Report Fraud. Do not assume that a bank-code delay alone means a SIM swap.

Frequently asked questions

Why aren't my UK bank verification codes arriving?

Possible causes include weak signal, phone settings, filtered messages, or a delay at the bank or mobile network. Try the basic checks, then contact the bank through the app or the number on your card if the problem continues.

How do I know if a 'bank' text is real or a scam?

A mismatched sender is a warning sign, but a matching name is not proof because sender IDs can be spoofed or hijacked. Do not tap an unexpected link asking you to log in or verify. Check the account in the official app or contact the bank yourself, and forward a suspicious text to 7726.

Can I get my verification codes without SMS at all?

Some banks and services provide app-based approval or authenticator options, but availability depends on the provider and account. Check the official app or help centre for the account concerned.

My HMRC, Microsoft, or Google code isn't arriving — does the same advice apply?

Yes, the universal fixes work for any service that sends verification codes by SMS. Reboot first, check signal and Do Not Disturb, and look for the message in any junk or filtered folder. Most major services also offer app-based or voice alternatives that bypass SMS entirely — for UK government services, sign in at gov.uk and switch your verification method in your Government Gateway settings. For Google, Apple, and Microsoft accounts, set up an authenticator app for codes that work even with no signal.

Fast checks

  • Pause before sending money or credentials
  • Verify with an official site, app, or number
  • Never share one-time passcodes
  • Be sceptical of bank transfer pressure
